newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-ATHENS MAY HAVE TO BEWARE OF GREEKS BEARING BANNERS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-ATHENS MAY HAVE TO BEWARE OF GREEKS BEARING BANNERS.

text.p: Athletics officials may be forced to take action against supporters of Athens' bid for the 2004 Olympics after scores of people held up a huge banner during Saturday's opening day of the world championships.
The International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) does not allow advertising from any of the five cities bidding for the Games in the stadium at the championships.
But spectators held up a banner promoting the Athens bid over scores of seats which was clearly visible on live television around the world.
Although the people who held it above their heads were not directly linked to the Athens bid, IAAF general secretary Istvan Gyulai described the banner as "excessive."

"If it happens again in the future we will have to discuss it," Gyulai said. "There is no rule on this. But our policy is not to accept advertising from a bidding committee. (But) There has been no official protest (to Athens)."
Athens, which is bidding against Rome, Buenos Aires, Cape Town and Stockholm for the Games, said it believed the supporters were volunteers from a local newspaper which is backing the bid.
"It has nothing to do with the Athens bidding committee. They bought the tickets and put up the banner," an Athens 2004 official said. "I believe they have the right to do that."

Athens is staging the most prestigious athletics event outside of the Olympic Games at a key moment in the bidding process. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) will decide next month on the hosts of the 2004 Summer Games.
The Greek capital is regarded as being a serious threat to favourites Rome and what happens at the world championships could influence the outcome of the vote.
The attendances in the first three sessions of the event have been disappointing.
Barely more than 3,000 people watched Michael Johnson start his 400 metres campaign on Sunday morning and the stadium was not filled during the evening session on Saturday.

"This has surprised us since we were told that 75 per cent of the tickets had been sold," Gyulai said. "I was flabbergasted (by the low numbers). But we will have to see if it is an exceptional case."
